problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###  

**a. Verdict** – I have obtained a complete solution.  
The minimum possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Permutation of uncovered squares.**  
   Let \(n=2025\).  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares is a permutation matrix: there is a bijection  

   \[
   p:\{1,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,\dots ,n\},
   \qquad\text{row }i\text{ has its uncovered cell at column }p(i).
   \]

2. **Two monotone regions.**  
   For every row \(i\) the squares left of the uncovered one form the *left region*  

   \[
   L=\{(i,j):j<p(i)\},
   \]

   and the squares right of it form the *right region*  

   \[
   R=\{(i,j):j>p(i)\}.
   \]

   Any axis‑parallel rectangle that avoids all uncovered squares must be completely contained in \(L\) **or** completely contained in \(R\); otherwise it would intersect the uncovered square of the row in which it crosses the vertical line \(x=p(i)\).

3. **A corner‑covering lemma.**  
   Order the rows so that  

   \[
   p(r_1)<p(r_2)<\dots <p(r_n).
   \]

   For each row \(r_k\) with \(p(r_k)>1\) the cell  

   \[
   c_k=(r_k,\,p(r_k)-1)
   \]

   is the right‑most cell of that row inside \(L\).  
   These \(n-1\) cells are called the **outer corners** of \(L\) (the unique row with \(p(r)=1\) has no left side).

   **Lemma.** *A rectangle contained in \(L\) can contain at most one outer corner.*  

   *Proof.*  
   Suppose a rectangle \(Q\subseteq L\) contains two distinct outer corners  
   \((r_a,p(r_a)-1)\) and \((r_b,p(r_b)-1)\) with \(p(r_a)<p(r_b)\).  
   The column interval of \(Q\) therefore contains every column from \(p(r_a)-1\) up to \(p(r_b)-1\); in particular it contains column \(p(r_a)\).  
   Row \(r_a\) together with column \(p(r_a)\) is precisely the uncovered square of row \(r_a\), which lies on the line \(x=p(r_a)\).  
   Because \(Q\) also contains row \(r_a\), the uncovered square would belong to \(Q\), contradicting the definition of \(L\). ∎  

   Consequently each outer corner must be covered by a distinct rectangle, so at least \(n-1\) rectangles are needed to cover the whole left region \(L\).

   An identical argument applied to the right region \(R\) (using the left‑most cells \((r_k,p(r_k)+1)\) of each row) shows that at least another \(n-1\) rectangles are required for \(R\).

   Hence **any** tiling uses at least  

   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
   \]

   rectangles.

4. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   Choose the *cyclic* permutation  

   \[
   p(i)=\begin{cases}
   i+1 & (1\le i\le n-1),\\[2pt]
   1   & (i=n).
   \end{cases}
   \]

   For each row \(i\) (\(1\le i\le n-1\)) place a horizontal tile covering the left part of the row:

   \[
   L_i=\{(i,j):1\le j\le i\}.
   \]

   For each row \(i\) (\(1\le i\le n-2\)) place a horizontal tile covering the right part of the row:

   \[
   R_i=\{(i,j):i+2\le j\le n\},
   \]

   and for the last row \(i=n\) place

   \[
   R_n=\{(n,j):2\le j\le n\}.
   \]

   *Verification.*  

   *Uncovered squares.*  
   By construction the uncovered square in row \(i\) (\(i<n\)) is \((i,i+1)\); in row \(n\) it is \((n,1)\). Thus each column also contains exactly one uncovered square (column \(j\) is uncovered in row \(j-1\) for \(j>1\), and column 1 is uncovered in row \(n\)).  

   *Tiles are disjoint.*  
   Every tile lies entirely in a single row, so no two tiles intersect.  

   *Coverage.*  
   In row \(i<n\) the union \(L_i\cup R_i\) covers all cells except the single uncovered cell \((i,i+1)\). In row \(n\) the union \(L_n\) is empty (because \(p(n)=1\)) and \(R_n\) covers all cells except \((n,1)\). Hence every unit square of the grid is either covered by exactly one tile or is one of the prescribed uncovered squares.  

   *Count of tiles.*  
   The left‑hand tiles \(L_i\) give \(n-1\) rectangles.  
   The right‑hand tiles consist of \(R_i\) for \(i=1,\dots ,n-2\) (that is \(n-2\) rectangles) together with \(R_n\) (one more), totalling again \(n-1\) rectangles.  

   Therefore the construction uses exactly  

   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
   \]

   tiles.

5. **Specialisation to the original grid.**  
   With \(n=2025\),

   \[
   2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
   \]

   The construction above provides an explicit placement of 4048 tiles satisfying all conditions, and the lower‑bound argument shows that no tiling can use fewer tiles.

Hence the minimum number of tiles required is \(\boxed{4048}\).

---

### Detailed Solution ###  

Let \(n=2025\).  
We work with the set \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) of row indices and column indices.

---

#### 1.  Uncovered squares as a permutation  

Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, there exists a bijection  

\[
p:\{1,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]

such that the unique uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,p(i))\).  
Consequently column \(j\) is uncovered in the unique row \(i\) with \(p(i)=j\).

Define  

\[
L=\{(i,j):j<p(i)\},\qquad 
R=\{(i,j):j>p(i)\}.
\]

Thus every covered square belongs either to \(L\) or to \(R\); the two sets are disjoint.

---

#### 2.  Rectangles cannot cross the permutation  

Let \(Q\) be any axis‑parallel rectangle whose interior consists only of covered squares.  
If \(Q\) contained points from both \(L\) and \(R\), then there would be a row \(i\) such that \(Q\) contains a cell with column \(<p(i)\) and also a cell with column \(>p(i)\).  
Since the column interval of a rectangle is contiguous, column \(p(i)\) would also belong to that interval, and together with row \(i\) the uncovered square \((i,p(i))\) would lie inside \(Q\) – a contradiction.  

Hence every rectangle is **entirely** contained in \(L\) or **entirely** contained in \(R\).

---

#### 3.  Lower bound for the left region  

Re‑order the rows so that  

\[
p(r_1)<p(r_2)<\dots <p(r_n).
\]

For each \(k\) with \(p(r_k)>1\) define the cell  

\[
c_k=(r_k,\,p(r_k)-1).
\]

These are precisely the right‑most cells of the rows inside \(L\); there are exactly \(n-1\) of them because exactly one row satisfies \(p(r)=1\) and therefore has no cell left of its uncovered square.

**Lemma 1.** *A rectangle contained in \(L\) can contain at most one cell \(c_k\).*  

*Proof.*  
Assume a rectangle \(Q\subseteq L\) contains two distinct cells \(c_a\) and \(c_b\) with \(p(r_a)<p(r_b)\).  
The column interval of \(Q\) contains every integer from \(p(r_a)-1\) up to \(p(r_b)-1\); in particular it contains column \(p(r_a)\).  
Since row \(r_a\) is also in the row interval of \(Q\), the uncovered square \((r_a,p(r_a))\) would belong to \(Q\), contradicting \(Q\subseteq L\). ∎  

Every cell of \(L\) must be covered by some rectangle. In particular each outer corner \(c_k\) must belong to a rectangle, and by Lemma 1 distinct outer corners require distinct rectangles. Therefore at least \(n-1\) rectangles are necessary to cover the whole left region \(L\).

---

#### 4.  Lower bound for the right region  

Apply the same reasoning to the right region \(R\).  
For each row \(i\) with \(p(i)<n\) the left‑most cell of \(R\) is \((i,p(i)+1)\); there are again \(n-1\) such cells.  
An analogous lemma shows that a rectangle contained in \(R\) can contain at most one of them, whence at least \(n-1\) rectangles are needed for \(R\).

---

#### 5.  Global lower bound  

Since the rectangles covering \(L\) and those covering \(R\) are disjoint families, the total number of rectangles in any admissible tiling is at least  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2.
\]

---

#### 6.  Construction attaining the bound  

Take the cyclic permutation  

\[
p(i)=\begin{cases}
i+1 & (1\le i\le n-1),\\
1   & (i=n).
\end{cases}
\]

*Uncovered squares.*  
Row \(i\) (\(i<n\)) has uncovered cell \((i,i+1)\); row \(n\) has uncovered cell \((n,1)\).  
Thus each column \(j\) (\(j>1\)) is uncovered in row \(j-1\), and column 1 is uncovered in row \(n\).

*Tiles.*  

- For each \(i=1,\dots ,n-1\) place the horizontal rectangle  

  \[
  L_i=\{(i,j):1\le j\le i\}.
  \]

  This covers the whole left part of row \(i\) (all cells with column \(<p(i)\)).

- For each \(i=1,\dots ,n-2\) place the horizontal rectangle  

  \[
  R_i=\{(i,j):i+2\le j\le n\},
  \]

  covering the right part of row \(i\) (all cells with column \(>p(i)\)).

- Finally, for the last row \(i=n\) place  

  \[
  R_n=\{(n,j):2\le j\le n\},
  \]

  which is the right part of row \(n\).

*Verification.*  

1. **Disjointness.**  
   Every tile lies in a single row, and different rows are distinct, so no two tiles intersect.

2. **Coverage of all non‑uncovered squares.**  
   In row \(i<n\) the union \(L_i\cup R_i\) consists of all columns except \(i+1\), i.e. exactly the covered squares of that row.  
   In row \(n\) the union \(L_n\cup R_n\) (with \(L_n\) empty) consists of all columns except \(1\).  
   Hence every unit square that is not one of the prescribed uncovered squares belongs to exactly one tile.

3. **Number of tiles.**  
   The left‑hand family \(\{L_i\}_{i=1}^{n-1}\) contributes \(n-1\) tiles.  
   The right‑hand family \(\{R_i\}_{i=1}^{n-2}\cup\{R_n\}\) also contributes \(n-1\) tiles.  
   Total: \(2n-2\) tiles.

Thus the construction uses exactly the lower‑bound number of tiles.

---

#### 7.  Conclusion for the original grid  

With \(n=2025\),

\[
2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
\]

Therefore the smallest possible number of rectangular tiles that can be placed under the given conditions is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]
